## Concepts and intuitions {.unnumbered} -->

::: {style="margin-top: 1em; font-size: 125%; font-weight: 1000; text-align: center;"}
Tsisy idiran'ny qualité!

As we move forward, the dependence previous because more crucial, but such could also faciliate the concept.
Here, a qualitative variable is just a a variable that is **NOT** quantitative @sec-quantitative-variable.

There is an inherent paradox with understanding and use of qualitative variables. On one hand, the preclivity of our brain to categorize stuff: male or female, good or bad, species, or even the creation of countries and boundaries. We like "qualitative" variable. On the other hand, most of the foundational mathematics and statistics we handle are about numbers, operation and etc. So we could dislike them because we don't know what kind of statistics do we do when the values are not numbers.

There are some that many students get when the variable is not fuzzy: sex or eye color or species. It becomes fuzzy when the qualitative variables are derived from quantitative variables. It is fuzzy because (1) we then to ignore the underlying quantitative variables (2) because the delimitation are forgotten. Think baby, juvenile, adult the underlying is age but there is no universal distinction among then. Think that these age class also apply to any living organism. Another is low, intermediate, or high elevation where the underlying is altitude but ...so we understand what one is talking about.

A final misconception is that (should be obvious from the paragraphs above): qualitative variable has nothing to do with quality. If one can switch to categorical variable, life could be easier.


## Formal {.unnumbered}
<!--
In statistics textbooks, a qualitative variable (often referred to interchangeably as a categorical variable) is defined as a variable that yields non-numerical attributes or places observational units into distinct categories based on a specific characteristic. Crucially, its defining mathematical feature is that arithmetic operations (like addition or finding an average) are meaningless.

Here are the rigorous definitions from three highly respected and widely used statistics textbooks. -->

<!-- 1. The Definitive Introductory/Applied Definition
In foundational applied statistics, a qualitative variable is defined explicitly by its inability to be measured numerically, instead serving to classify subjects. -->

<!-- Textbook Source
Book: Introductory Statistics (10th Edition)
Author: Neil A. Weiss
Publisher: Pearson -->

The Definition
In Chapter 1 ("The Nature of Statistics"), Weiss provides a highly structured breakdown of variable types:
"Variables can be classified as either qualitative or quantitative. A qualitative variable (or categorical variable) is a non-numerically valued variable that classifies an attribute of each individual element of a population or sample. The values of a qualitative variable are typically words or codes, and arithmetic operations do not make sense for them."


There can be three types: nominal, ordinal, or binary. Nominal is when the values have no inherent order, this is in contrast with ordinal where there is sense of order (baby, teenager, adult, etc.). Note that many ordinal are obtained from binning of a quantitative variable @sec-quantiative-variable. Binary is a special case of qualitative variable that has only two categories  (yes and no, 0 or 1, true or false, male or female etc.) @sec-boolean

## Examples {.unnumbered}

- Nominal variable:
  - nationality (Malagasy, English, Kenyan etc.)
  - Political party (Democrat, Republican, Independent)
  - Eye color (blue, brown, green)
  - Species name
  - Zip code: 101, 102, 303 etc.

Notice in the last example, zip code is a number but it is not a quantitative variable. You cannot do arithmetic operation on it. It is just a label.

- Ordinal variable that has intrinsic numerical value behind it:
  - Education level (high school, bachelor's, master's, PhD)
  - Customer satisfaction (very dissatisfied, dissatisfied, neutral, satisfied, very satisfied)
  - Egg size (small, medium, large)

In the example above, you don't explicity grade your satisfaction but you sort of arbirarily assign a category. It could also be 0, 1, 2, 3 etc...Does it make sense to average it? Not really. But you can say that 3 is better than 2, and 2 is better than 1. So there is a sense of order.

- Ordinal variable that has explicit numerical value behind it:
  - Age group (child, teenager, adult, senior)--age
  - Income bracket (low, medium, high) -- salary
  - Test score category (fail, pass, excellent) -- grade
  - Elevation category (lowland, upland, highland) -- altitude

- Binary variable:
  - Gender (male, female)
  - Yes/No questions (e.g., "Do you own a car?")

## Tips and warnings {.unnumbered}
- Plurality of notation: a qualitative variable can take many notations: For instance, in the column of dead or alive you can choose between: dead/alive, d/a, maty/velona, yes/no, Y/N, 1/0, oui/non/. For instance, 1/0 is not quantitative. Differentiate between the notation and the value. You cannot choose for quantitative.
- Collecting qualitative is often efficient. But this is a trade-off. When possible record the quantitative and convert to qualitative. You can't do that in reverse.
- A natural divide is what kind of visualization uses, you cannot use a histogram for qualitative variable.
- A binary qualitative can always be encoded as yes or no, true or false question. Variable color: Blue or red vs variable: Is it blue? : value = true or false. It is often convenient to use boolean variables as they are specifically created to two values. @sec-boolean
- Using 0 and 1 does not make it numeric.

3. The Comprehensive "Mathematical/Applied" Hybrid Definition
Even in engineering and hard science contexts, qualitative variables are defined strictly by the descriptive categories they generate.

Textbook Source
Book: Probability and Statistics for Engineering and the Sciences (9th Edition, 2016)
Author: Jay L. Devore
Publisher: Cengage Learning

The Definition
In Chapter 1, Devore explicitly separates variables by the mathematical properties of their outputs:
"A qualitative variable is one for which the possible values are distinct categories rather than numbers. Examples include gender (male or female), method of payment (cash, check, or credit card), and type of defect. When a variable is qualitative, the resulting data is a collection of labels or category names."
Core Structural Classifications of Qualitative Variables

As outlined across these textbooks, qualitative variables are rigorously divided into sub-types based on their measurement scales:
 -Nominal Scale: Categories have no inherent mathematical order or ranking (e.g., Blood Type: A, B, AB, O; Eye Color: Blue, Brown, Green).
- Ordinal Scale: Categories possess a natural, logical order, but the "distance" between the categories cannot be measured numerically (e.g., Customer Satisfaction: Poor, Fair, Good, Excellent).
- Dichotomous / Binary Scale: A special case of a qualitative variable that contains exactly two mutually exclusive categories (e.g., Pass/Fail, Yes/No).

A Note on "Fake" Numbers: Textbooks frequently warn that qualitative variables can sometimes look like numbers (e.g., Zip Codes, Area Codes, or coding Male as 0 and Female as 1). They remain strictly qualitative because calculating the "average zip code" yields a mathematically meaningless result. -->
